Gastrointestinal Disorders

Esophageal Emergencies

Esophageal complaints range from outpatient dysphagia and reflux to airway-threatening food impaction, button battery injury, and mediastinitis from perforation. ED priorities are to separate cardiac mimics, airway risk, complete obstruction, caustic/sharp battery emergencies, and perforation from stable outpatient disease.

Board trap: Antacid response does not rule out ACS, and a patient who cannot handle secretions has a time-sensitive obstruction.

ESOPHAGEAL EMERGENCIES

INTRODUCTION

Dysphagia, odynophagia, foreign body sensation, chest pain, upper GI bleeding, malignancy, and mediastinitis can all implicate the esophagus. Most reflux or dysphagia workups can occur outpatient, but foreign body obstruction and perforation demand active ED management.

ANATOMY AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

The esophagus is a muscular mediastinal tube with cervical and abdominal components. Anatomic narrowing at the cricopharyngeus, aortic arch, left main bronchus, and lower sphincter explains where foreign bodies lodge. The esophagus has no serosa, so perforation can rapidly contaminate mediastinum, pleura, or peritoneum.

Tintinalli source

Figure 77-1

Anatomic relations of the esophagus.

DYSPHAGIA

Oropharyngeal dysphagia causes drooling, gagging, nasal regurgitation, repeated swallowing, aspiration risk, and difficulty initiating a swallow. Esophageal dysphagia causes food sticking or retrosternal fullness after swallowing begins. Solids-first progression suggests mechanical obstruction; solids-and-liquids from the start suggests motility disease.

Tintinalli source

Table 77-1

Causes of dysphagia.

GASTROESOPHAGEAL REFLUX DISEASE

GERD occurs when reflux becomes symptomatic or injures upper GI or airway mucosa. Transient lower-sphincter relaxation, low sphincter pressure, decreased motility, and delayed gastric emptying contribute. ED treatment is acid suppression and risk-factor advice, but ACS must be excluded when the presentation fits cardiac disease.

Tintinalli source

Table 77-2

Causes of gastroesophageal reflux disease.

ESOPHAGITIS

Esophagitis causes prolonged chest pain and almost always odynophagia. Etiologies include GERD, pills, eosinophilic inflammation, infection, radiation, caustics, and foreign body injury. Pill offenders include NSAIDs, potassium chloride, doxycycline/tetracycline/clindamycin, and bisphosphonates. Infectious esophagitis in an otherwise healthy patient should prompt immune-status evaluation.

ESOPHAGEAL PERFORATION

Iatrogenic instrumentation is most common. Boerhaave syndrome is full-thickness rupture after abrupt pressure rise from vomiting, coughing, straining, seizure, or childbirth, usually distal and left-sided. Trauma, caustics, foreign bodies, infection, tumor, and aortic pathology also occur.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Leakage into mediastinum, pleura, or peritoneum can cause fulminant mediastinitis, pneumonitis, peritonitis, shock, or abscess. A small contained leak may be indolent; thoracic/distal contamination is more dangerous.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Classic pain is acute, severe, unrelenting, diffuse chest/neck/abdominal pain, worse with swallowing, radiating to back or shoulders. Tachycardia, tachypnea, fever, hypotension, abdominal rigidity, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, cervical subcutaneous emphysema, and Hamman's crunch may appear. Delayed diagnosis sharply worsens morbidity and mortality.

DIAGNOSIS

Obtain early surgical consultation when seriously suspected. CT neck/chest/abdomen, water-soluble contrast esophagography, and endoscopy/esophagoscopy are chosen by stability and local expertise. If water-soluble study is negative but suspicion remains, follow with barium when appropriate.

TREATMENT

Keep NPO, resuscitate, give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, drain contaminated spaces when needed, and involve surgery early. Stable, small, contained cervical perforations may be managed conservatively only with close monitoring and a surgeon immediately available.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Most patients require admission, often ICU-level monitoring, with surgical or thoracic consultation. Do not discharge suspected perforation because deterioration may be abrupt.

SWALLOWED FOREIGN BODIES AND FOOD IMPACTION

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Children 18 to 48 months, psychiatric patients, prisoners, adults with esophageal disease, dementia, and edentulous adults are high-risk groups. Objects wider than 2.5 cm, longer than 6 cm, sharp/irregular objects, button batteries, magnets, and esophageal impactions are dangerous.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Adults usually give a clear history with retrosternal pain, dysphagia, vomiting, choking, or localization. Children may present with refusal to eat, gagging, stridor, neck/throat pain, drooling, vomiting, or unexplained respiratory findings. Airway assessment comes first.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen Ch.75 adds practical ED distinctions: pediatric airway anatomy and entrapment levels, coin-versus-button-battery x-ray details, and perforation imaging examples. Tintinalli Ch.77 supplies the chapter spine, urgent-endoscopy criteria, button-battery algorithm, and disposition rules.

DIAGNOSIS

Use AP/lateral neck, chest, and abdominal films for radiopaque objects. Esophageal coins show the circular face on AP films; tracheal coins tend to show the face on lateral films. CT is high yield for nonradiopaque objects, bones, and suspected perforation. Food bolus x-rays are often low yield.

TREATMENT

ENDOSCOPY

Emergent endoscopy is required for complete obstruction, inability to manage secretions, airway compromise, button battery, sharp/elongated object, multiple objects, perforation, cricopharyngeal coin in a child, or object present more than 24 hours. Advanced imaging should not delay clearly indicated endoscopy.

LARYNGOSCOPY

Very proximal objects may be removed with direct visualization, Magill forceps, Kelly clamp, indirect laryngoscopy, or fiberoptic scope in stable patients.

EXPECTANT TREATMENT

Objects distal to pylorus that are benign in shape/nature, with a comfortable patient tolerating PO, can often be observed. Worrisome distal objects need surgical or GI input and documented passage.

FOLEY CATHETER REMOVAL

Foley catheter or bougienage techniques are alternatives for selected blunt foreign bodies present less than 24 hours without structural disease or perforation, and require experienced operators and airway backup.

GLUCAGON

Glucagon 1-2 mg IV may be tried for distal esophageal food bolus, but success is poor and likely no better than watchful waiting. It must not delay endoscopy when obstruction is complete or high risk.

FOOD IMPACTION

Meat is the commonest food bolus. Complete obstruction or bony fragments require emergency endoscopy. Uncomplicated partial impaction may pass with time/sedation, but should not remain impacted more than 12-24 hours. Papain/meat tenderizer is contraindicated because it can injure mucosa and cause perforation.

COIN INGESTION

Many centers remove esophageal coins endoscopically. Foley catheter removal under fluoroscopy can work in selected cases with airway management immediately available.

BUTTON BATTERY INGESTION

A button battery lodged in the esophagus is a true emergency. Necrosis and perforation can occur within hours, especially with lithium cells. If past the esophagus and asymptomatic, observation requires reliable follow-up and repeat films.

Tintinalli source

Figure 77-3

Algorithm for management of button battery ingestion.

INGESTION OF SHARP OBJECTS

Sharp objects in the esophagus need immediate removal; sharp objects in stomach/duodenum should be removed endoscopically when possible. If distal to duodenum and asymptomatic, document passage with daily films and call surgery if symptoms or no progression.

NARCOTICS INGESTION

Body packers may carry lethal packets. Endoscopy is contraindicated because packet rupture can be fatal. Observe intact packets with surgical/toxicology involvement; whole-bowel irrigation may be used in selected cases.
